Maya: fyi noticed a CPU-side regression after the kernel-selection change pushed yesterday — latency p50 for small prompts up ~20% and CPU sat on token_splitter/sched wake paths
Liam: which workload? e2e benchmark or dev harness?
Maya: repro is on our ingestion microbench (50 concurrent short requests, seq len ~64). Runs on dedicated dev GPUs but the spike is purely on the CPU thread (tokenization / batching logic)
Jen: curious if kernel picker changed the batching heuristic and added an extra prefix copy? any perf trace?
Maya: captured a quick perf + flamegraph on the worker. attaching snippet below. main hotspots: token_splitter::split_fragments, Scheduler::wake_if_needed, futex_wait (syscall), and a surprising amount in python-level glue (PyObject_Call).
Maya: ```
# perf top sampling summary (2s window)
rank  symbol                              pct
1     token_splitter::split_fragments     27.1
2     Scheduler::wake_if_needed           15.4
3     __futex_wait                        12.2
4     PyObject_Call                       8.3
5     batching::maybe_flush               6.9
```
Liam: that futex churn + Scheduler wake screams lock-contention. Did the kernel picker switch to a different batching path that uses a mutex per-request?
Oli: looking at the diff, the picker will force per-stream KV cache fence for certain kernels to avoid stale KV reuse. That added a fence in split_fragments when a kernel variant mismatch is detected. Could explain extra locks.
Jen: can we reproduce with perf record --call-graph dwarf so we get Python frames? want to confirm whether C++ lock or Python callback is the real culprit.
Maya: did a longer trace with perf record + flamegraph (attached). Here's a collapsed sample of heavy stacks (simplified):
Maya: ```
token_splitter::split_fragments; Scheduler::wake_if_needed; __futex_wait
PyObject_Call; batching::maybe_flush; runtime::submit_kernel
```
Maya: interestingly, when I run the same bench with kernel-picker disabled (revert to old selection), the futex and wake paths drop by ~70% and p50 latency returns to baseline.
Liam: so picker change likely introduced a hot path that serializes some work. We should examine the code path where we detect kernel-variant != active and then call into Python (for model metadata) — that could be a blocking syscall or GIL hold.
Jen: do we have a perfetto timeline from the same run? kernel timelines might show thread switching/blocked durations vs compute.
Maya: yes. Perfetto shows repeated short blocks (~3-7ms) where the CPU thread is in syscall wait between GPU submits. Batcher threads spike at same time trying to acquire the same mutex.
Oli: I'll instrument the fence path to avoid Python-level callbacks: push a C++ fast-path that caches kernel variant decisions and defers policy re-eval to background task. Minimal change: avoid calling back into model_metadata fetch while holding the batching lock.
Liam: also consider changing the batching heuristic back to optimistic append (no fence) and then do compatibility check asynchronously. If correctness still preserved, that may remove the sync point.
Maya: quick micro-patch: moved metadata lookup off critical section and added an atomic cached_variant; re-ran bench -> futex% drops from 12.2 to 3.1, p50 back to baseline +/-2%
Jen: nice. Can you paste the small diff we used for the experiment?
Maya: ```diff
diff --git a/runtime/batching.cpp b/runtime/batching.cpp
@@
-  std::lock_guard g(lock_);
-  auto meta = model_metadata_lookup_sync(key);
-  if (meta.variant != active) {
-    fence_and_switch(meta.variant);
-  }
+  std::lock_guard g(lock_);
+  // capture key, but do not call out to blocking metadata fetch while locked
+  auto key_copy = key;
+  g.~lock_guard(); // manual unlock
+  auto meta = model_metadata_lookup_async_cached(key_copy);
+  if (meta.variant != active) {
+    std::lock_guard g2(lock_);
+    fence_and_switch(meta.variant);
+  }
```
Liam: eh manual destructor is ugly but fine for quick experiment. We should refactor into helper methods. Also need to be careful about time-of-check/time-of-use races if variant changes while unlocked.
Maya: agreed — the async_cached lookup returns an in-memory cached variant immediately most of the time so we avoid expensive path; fallback still goes through safe fenced path.
perf-bot: benchmark/ingest-microbench: regression-check: baseline -> current: p50 +19.6% before patch, +1.2% after patch (experimental branch)
Jen: next steps: Oli to propose a proper API: try_get_cached_variant() that is O(1) and never blocks; background task updates cache and triggers safe rollouts. Add unit tests for race scenarios. Also need e2e run on dedicated cluster (can't just trust dev machine).
Oli: will open PR with design doc + perf numbers. I'll also add a perf suite that includes perf record + flamegraph for the critical path so regression gating can catch this class.
Liam: good. Also add a tracing span around kernel selection so we can see these stalls in our production traces (x-request-id correlated).
Maya: logging note: capture sample stack traces periodically (perf or pstack) on canary to catch future regressions quicker.
Jen: sounds like a plan. Thanks for the quick bisect and patch. :thumbsup:
Maya: thanks — will follow up with PR link and perf artifacts.
